planting.note: Divide rhizomes in fall and plant in deep, humus-rich soil tucked among larger shrubs or at the edge of a conifer canopy with dappled light; keep soil consistently moist through the first growing season.

directions: An extremely rare Pacific Northwest woodland endemic restricted to roughly three counties along the Clackamas River drainage in Oregon, this iris offers genuine shade tolerance combined with a fast colonizing habit, making it a distinctive native groundcover under conifers or big-leaf maple. Established colonies spread quickly to three feet across via creeping rhizomes, so it works well as a native shade groundcover rather than a specimen plant. Division in fall is the fastest and most reliable way to build new colonies, since seed-grown plants are slow to flower and viable seed can be hard to source given how restricted the species' wild range is.
sources: Species Iris Group of North America
